doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

chapter: Studio philosophy: making the artist comfortable
title: Tapestry and eye contact in the rhythm section
summary: Asked if Tapestry felt like a hit, Hank says they felt it from the start, and repeats why players need eye contact.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Can I ask you about “Tapestry” and did you have a feeling with that record in particular that this was going to be a hit?

I’ll tell you, having done a lot of albums all those years you get a feeling once in a while about an album, this is going to be good. Generally you say this is good but they never quite make it. “Tapestry” was, right from the go we felt it. And my method of setting up an orchestra or a band — well not an orchestra, that’s a different situation — but a rhythm section, a couple of guitars, piano and drums — I tried to make them — surround them, so that they could all see each other. I hated that thing where you put the drums are in a booth and you want them in a booth, that’s fine. Then build the rest of the band around the booth so they all can see each other. These dates, they’re stiff when you put the drummer in a booth and then you put the two guitar players on the other side of the room somewhere and the bass player he’s somewhere else and has no contact with the drummer. Those dates are stiff. They don’t work for me. My feeling has always been that they all have eye contact — I’m sorry — with the rhythm section but they all have eye contact with the artist. I would put the artist in the middle of the room with the whole © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

band sitting around it made, for him, it made them feel more comfortable because they had more contact. You put everybody in the booth — the drummer’s over in this booth and the singer’s in that booth, and the guys are here — it never felt right to me you know, because those poor guys are all sitting in a room playing and there’s no eye contact. They don’t see each other.
